title: Effect of turning and abrasive finishing processes on surface integrity in supermartensitic stainless steel
abstract: Abstract Machining induced residual stresses and surface finish play an important role on the integrity and performance of the machined components. This work aims to investigate the behavior of residual stresses induced by turning followed by grinding and belt-finishing of supermartensitic stainless steel using different cutting conditions. Analyses of residual stresses were conducted by X-ray diffraction technique, using the sin²ψ method. Layer removal by electropolishing was used to assess the subsurface residual stresses and measurements of surface roughness complemented the study. The main contribution of this study is the experimental investigation of how turning and post-turning finishing operations modify surface and subsurface residual stress states in supermartensitic stainless steel, providing practical insights into surface integrity control in machined components. The results show that turning with wiper insert in combination with belt-finishing with finer abrasive belt produced the highest compressive residual stresses on the surface, as well as an affected layer along which the compressive residual stresses were more stable. Grinding also produced surface compressive residual stresses, however, tensile residual stresses of low magnitudes were obtained in the subsurface layers. Regarding surface finish, turning with wiper inserts, lower feed rates and higher cutting speeds resulted in lower Ra values and feed rate showed to influence more expressively on Ra than cutting speed. Both grinding and belt-finishing processes resulted in better surface finish compared to turning, but no expressive difference was observed between the finishing operations.
journal: Journal of the Brazilian Society of Mechanical Sciences and Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In machining processes, the workpiece is subjected to severe mechanical and thermal loads that promote plastic deformation, heat generation and, depending on the cutting conditions and workpiece material properties, microstructural modifications in the near-surface region. These phenomena induce residual stresses, whose magnitude and distribution depend on both the machining parameters and the dominant material removal mechanisms [ 1 ]. Residual stresses are the stresses that remain in a component after manufacturing, in the absence of external thermomechanical loads [ 2 ]. These stresses play a critical role in the functional performance of machined components, as they can either enhance or deteriorate properties such as fatigue life, wear resistance and susceptibility to stress corrosion cracking [ 3 ]. In this context, tensile residual stresses, generally associated with thermally dominated processes, are known to be detrimental to structural integrity, whereas compressive residual stresses, typically associated with mechanically dominated mechanisms, are often beneficial [ 4 ]. In addition to residual stresses, surface roughness is another critical aspect of surface integrity, strongly influencing the mechanical performance of machined components [ 5 ]. The combined effect of surface topography and residual stress state becomes particularly relevant in engineering components where surface integrity governs service life.

Turning is one of the most common machining processes and the residual stresses and surface finish produced on turned components depend on different cutting conditions such as cutting tool geometry and cutting parameters [ 6 ]. In terms of cutting tool geometry, the wiper technology consists of an optimized geometry in which the nose of the insert is composed of multiple small radii, resulting in an effectively larger nose radius, as opposed to conventional geometry consisting of a single nose radius. This optimized nose geometry enables machining with higher feed rates, which results in higher productivity, and at the same time produces a high surface quality [ 7 ]. Abbas et al. [ 8 ]. conducted a comparative study of surface quality, tool wear and specific energy for wiper and conventional carbide inserts in hard turning of AISI 4340 steel. The authors observed a drastic reduction in surface roughness (Ra) when turning with wiper insert, compared to conventional inserts, higher values of flank wear for conventional inserts and higher specific energy required by wiper inserts. Guddat et al. [ 9 ]. investigated the surface integrity in hard turning of AISI 52,100 steel using PCBN wiper and conventional geometry inserts. The authors stated that higher thermomechanical loads were induced by wiper inserts due to their bigger contact area, which was associated with higher forces (Fr and Ft). They observed that the use of wiper inserts leads to higher compressive residual stresses, as well as lower surface roughness, when compared to conventional inserts, characterizing a better surface integrity. In a study conducted by Kurinawan et al. [ 10 ]. the tool life and surface integrity were analyzed in hard turning of AISI 420 martensitic stainless steel. The authors observed that compressive residual stresses were generated when turning with the lowest levels of cutting speed (100 m/min) and feed (0.125 mm/rev), but the stresses shifted to tensile with the highest levels (170 m/min and 0.25 mm/rev). It was observed that the increase in cutting speed or in feed lead to a transition from continuous to segmented chip, the latter being involved with higher temperature during cutting, which is associated to thermally induced tensile residual stresses. Bashir et al. [ 11 ]. investigated the performance of wiper ceramic inserts on dry turning by different cutting parameters. It was observed that the surface roughness decreased when increasing cutting speed from 100 m/min to 210 m/min, keeping feed rate at lowest level of 0.05 mm/rev, whereas higher values of surface roughness were obtained with lower cutting speed and higher feed rate.

It is well known that cutting speed and feed play an important role in determining the surface integrity of turned components. However, the exact effect of these cutting parameters on the resulting residual stresses is not well defined. The evolution of the residual stresses in sequential cutting turning was numerically and experimentally investigated by Weng et al. [ 12 ]. Tensile residual stresses were obtained and, independent of the conditions, the stresses increased with an increase in feed, which was associated to higher forces and temperatures observed for higher values of feed. Stenberg and Proudian [ 13 ] proposed a numerical model for finding residual stresses in turning and the results showed that compressive residual stresses were generated by the model considering a feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev, tool rake angle of 6º and cutting speed varying from 40 m/min to 400 m/min. However, the stresses decreased in magnitude with an increase in cutting speed up to 260 m/min, increasing again with the highest cutting speed of 400 m/min. Sarnobat and Raval [ 14 ] analyzed the residual stresses and surface roughness in turning of AISI D2 steel. Tensile stresses were generated in all conditions, however, a decrease in the magnitude of the stresses in the axial direction was observed when increasing cutting speed and feed rate. As for the surface finish, it was observed that an increase in cutting speed first lead to higher values of surface roughness and then lower values of roughness with the highest cutting speed, whereas only increasing values of roughness were obtained with increasing feed rate. Salman et al. [ 15 ]. investigated the effect of cutting parameters on turning of AISI 1035 alloy. They found that increasing cutting speed resulted in less tensile residual stresses, but increasing feed rate resulted in tensile residual stresses of higher magnitudes.

Grinding is a well-established abrasive finishing process, commonly employed as the final step in the manufacturing of a wide range of mechanical components, directly influencing their surface integrity and in-service performance [ 16 ]. The process produces fine surface finishes, typically characterized by low roughness values [ 17 ]. The friction due to the action of abrasive particles of the grinding wheel leads to intense thermal effects inducing tensile residual stresses. At the same time, the normal contact force applied by the grinding wheel may cause elastic or plastic deformations resulting in compressive residual stresses, depending on factors such as cutting conditions and workpiece material [ 16 ].

During grinding, the interaction between abrasive grains and the workpiece gives rise to complex thermo-mechanical phenomena. Frictional effects and plastic deformation within the wheel–workpiece contact zone generate intense heat, which may lead to thermally induced tensile residual stresses at the surface. Conversely, the normal contact forces applied by abrasive grains can promote elastic and plastic deformation, often resulting in mechanically induced compressive residual stresses. The final residual stress state therefore reflects a balance between thermal and mechanical contributions, being strongly dependent on grinding parameters, wheel characteristics, cooling conditions, and workpiece material properties [ 16 ,  17 – 18 ]. According to comprehensive reviews by Ding et al. [ 17 ]. and Gong et al. [ 16 ], mechanically dominated regimes, typically associated with higher normal forces or lower temperatures, promote compressive stress states, whereas thermally dominated grinding conditions tend to favor tensile surface residual stresses. In many practical situations, both mechanisms act simultaneously, leading to different residual stress profiles, depending on cutting conditions and workpiece material properties.

In the work conducted by Kebede et al. [ 19 ], the authors investigated the effects of successive grinding and burnishing on surface roughness and residual stresses of additively manufactured stainless steel, both at the surface and on the subsurface. The results showed that grinding led to a significant reduction in surface roughness compared to the as-built condition and altered the residual stress state, promoting a transition toward more compressive stresses at the surface. The authors also reported that the residual stress distribution varied with depth, indicating that the material removal and plastic deformation induced during grinding played an important role in defining the resulting stress profile. In Jouini et al. [ 20 ], the authors investigated the influence of surface integrity on the fatigue life of AISI 52,100 bearing rings finished by precision hard turning and grinding. Regarding grinding, the results showed that it produced relatively low surface roughness, but induced a residual stress state characterized by compressive stresses at the surface followed by tensile residual stresses in the subsurface, starting at shallow depths. In contrast, precision hard turning generated subsurface compressive residual stresses at shallow depths. Furno and Sosa [ 21 ] investigated the influence of grinding parameters and microstructural features on surface roughness and residual stress in grinding of austempered ductile iron (ADI). Regarding residual stresses, the authors reported that the final stress state resulted from the balance between mechanical and thermal effects, with plastic deformation promoting compressive residual stresses and thermal effects favoring tensile stresses. The predominance of each mechanism depended on the selected cutting conditions, particularly wheel speed and workpiece speed, which influenced equivalent chip thickness, heat generation, and deformation depth. With respect to surface roughness, they observed that Ra increased with increasing wheel speed. In Zhang et al. [ 22 ], the authors compared dry hard turning and grinding as finishing processes for carburized 18CrNiMo7-6 steel, with emphasis on surface integrity and fatigue performance. For the grinding condition, they analyzed surface roughness and surface residual stresses as a function of grinding parameters, including workpiece speed and wheel feed rate. The results showed that grinding produced compressive residual stresses on the surface, whose magnitude depended on the balance between mechanical deformation and thermal effects, with higher wheel feed rates leading to a reduction in compressive stress due to increased grinding heat. Surface roughness was also affected by the grinding parameters, increasing with workpiece speed and exhibiting a minimum at intermediate wheel feed rates. Wang et al. [ 23 ]. studied the surface integrity of 300 M ultrahigh-strength steel subjected to different surface modification treatments, using ground samples as a reference condition. The grinding process produced a relatively shallow plastically deformed layer, with visible grinding marks and moderate surface roughness. Residual stress results showed that grinding induced compressive residual stresses of lower magnitude and limited penetration depth when compared to the subsequent surface modification treatments. The authors attributed this behavior to the lower plastic strain introduced by grinding compared the other processes, resulting in a comparatively thin compressive residual stress layer and reduced work hardening. In Furno and Sosa [ 24 ], the authors investigated the effects of grinding on the surface integrity of ductile iron with different microstructures. Surface roughness was evaluated through Ra and Rt parameters, showing that all ground surfaces exhibited roughness values within the typical range for grinding operations. Residual stress profiles were measured in the longitudinal direction and revealed predominantly compressive stresses at the surface for most microstructures, although ferritic samples exhibited tensile residual stresses with higher dispersion, attributed to increased friction and thermal effects during grinding. The authors discussed the balance between mechanical effects, responsible for compressive residual stresses through plastic deformation, and thermal effects, associated with tensile stresses, emphasizing that the resulting residual stress state strongly depends on the material microstructure under identical grinding conditions. In Jiang et al. [ 25 ], the authors investigated the influence of grinding parameters on grinding temperature, surface integrity and surface roughness during form grinding of quenched automotive transmission gears. The study focused on the effects of grinding depth, feed speed and grinding speed on grinding burn, white layer formation and surface roughness (Sa). The authors reported that increasing grinding depth led to a significant increase in grinding temperature and promoted severe grinding burn, characterized by the formation of thick white layers. Grinding depth was identified as the most influential parameter on surface roughness, with higher depths resulting in increased Sa values due to intensified plastic deformation and thermal effects at the grinding interface. The observed surface roughness was associated with deeper grooves, material pile-up and abrasive particle interactions, especially under more aggressive grinding conditions. Yin and Chen [ 26 ] studied the grindability and surface integrity of high-strength steel subjected to creep-feed grinding using grinding wheels. The study addressed surface roughness and residual stresses, analyzing the influence of grinding parameters, particularly grinding depth, wheel speed, and workpiece feed rate, on thermal damage and surface integrity. The authors reported that increasing grinding depth and feed rate intensified thermal effects, leading to higher surface roughness and the development of tensile residual stresses associated with grinding burns. In contrast, the use of CBN (cubic boron nitride) wheels promoted lower grinding temperatures, resulting in improved surface finish and predominantly compressive residual stress states, which were attributed to reduced thermal loading and enhanced heat dissipation. Biswas et al. [ 27 ]. experimentally analyzed the influence of grinding parameters and cutting conditions on surface roughness during surface grinding of EN24 alloy steel and mild steel. The study focused primarily on the effect of depth of cut under dry and wet grinding conditions. The results showed that surface roughness generally increased with increasing depth of cut for both materials, which the authors associated with higher heat generation and wheel loading at larger depths of cut. In addition, the use of coolant was reported to reduce surface roughness in most conditions when compared to dry grinding, emphasizing the role of thermal effects and lubrication in controlling surface quality during grinding. In the work conducted by Lerra et al. [ 28 ], the authors evaluated the surface integrity in dry grinding of automotive gears. The influence of grinding parameters such as feed rate, stock removal per pass and number of passes was investigated. The authors reported that higher feed rates led to increased surface roughness, while the use of multiple passes contributed to smoother surfaces by reducing the asperities generated in previous passes.

Superfinishing processes are also used to improve the surface integrity of mechanical components. Belt-finishing is one of these processes and has been widely implemented in many industries due to its capability of producing excellent surface finish, while at the same time inducing compressive residual stresses in the surface and subsurface layers of the finished components. In this process material is removed by the action of an abrasive belt pressed against the surface of the rotating workpiece by a polymer roller. The belt, which is fed by two rotating rollers composed of the fresh belt and the worn belt, scratches the workpiece surface with a feed speed and oscillates with certain frequency in the direction parallel to the workpiece axis [ 29 ]. Cherguy et al. [ 30 ]. investigated the influence of belt-finishing on the surface integrity and fatigue performance of 27MnCr5 carburized steel, comparing belt-finished samples with hard-turned ones. The results showed that belt-finishing induced compressive residual stresses in the near-surface region, in both axial and circumferential directions, while significantly reducing surface roughness when compared to hard turning. The authors emphasized that these compressive stresses were mainly concentrated within the first tens of micrometers below the surface and were associated with the predominance of mechanical scratching and limited heat generation during belt-finishing process. In Wang et al. [ 31 ], the authors investigated the residual stress state induced by dry belt-finishing applied after hard turning of AISI 52,100 bearing steel. The results showed that dry belt-finishing generated significant compressive residual stresses in the near-surface region, with a limited affected depth about a few micrometers. The influence of applied force was found to be negligible, which was attributed to the redistribution of the load among individual abrasive grits, while variations in finishing duration also showed no significant effect due to the competing mechanisms of stress accumulation and material removal at the surface. In a study conducted by Cherguy et al. [ 32 ], the authors investigated the influence of abrasive grain size on surface roughness and residual stress state induced by belt finishing of carburized 27MnCr5 steel shafts. The results showed that surface roughness was strongly dependent on grain size, with finer belts reducing roughness only by removing surface peaks, while intermediate grain sizes (around 20–30 μm) were able to remove the initial hard-turned texture and generate a new surface signature. Regarding residual stresses, belt-finishing introduced compressive stresses in the near-surface region for all grain sizes, with affected depths in the order of micrometers, while the magnitude and distribution of residual stresses did not show a clear dependence on grain size. Bouktib and Khellouki [ 29 ] studied the effect of belt-finishing on the residual stress field through a controlled repeated scratching approach applied to a rough hard-turned surface. The study focused on isolating the mechanical contribution of abrasive grain interactions, showing that repeated scratching progressively modified the residual stress state, promoting the development of compressive residual stresses near the surface. The results indicated that the magnitude and distribution of residual stresses were strongly related to the abrasive grain size and the number of scratching passes, emphasizing the role of mechanical deformation mechanisms during belt-finishing. In Hamdi et al. [ 33 ], the authors investigated the effect of abrasive grit size and minimum quantity lubrication (MQL) on the surface roughness generated during belt-grinding of a case-hardened steel. Surface quality was primarily evaluated through the Ra parameter. The results showed a clear reduction in surface roughness with decreasing abrasive grain size, indicating a strong correlation between grit size and surface texture. In a study conducted by Xiao et al. [ 34 ], the authors investigated the influence of abrasive belt-grinding parameters on surface integrity and fatigue performance of a GH4169 nickel-based superalloy. The study evaluated the effects of belt linear speed, feed speed and grinding depth on surface roughness and residual stress distributions. The authors reported that increasing belt speed and reducing grinding depth led to lower surface roughness, whereas higher feed speed and grinding depth promoted higher roughness values. Regarding residual stresses, compressive residual stresses were induced in all grinding conditions, with their magnitude and penetration depth increasing mainly with grinding depth and feed speed, which were associated with higher mechanical deformation and reduced thermal accumulation. Bouktib and Khellouki [ 35 ] studied the generation and evolution of residual stresses during belt-finishing of AISI 52,100 steel using a numerical multi-scratching approach. Finite element simulations were used to analyze the effects of abrasive grain size, initial surface roughness, and repeated scratching on the residual stress field. The results showed that increasing abrasive grain size promoted higher compressive residual stresses at the surface and extended the depth of the affected layer, while repeated scratching led to a progressive stabilization of the residual stress distribution. The authors also demonstrated that smoother initial surfaces favored higher compressive residual stresses after stabilization, with strain hardening identified as the dominant mechanism governing residual stress evolution during repeated abrasive interactions.

Supermartensitic stainless steels (SMSS) were developed as an evolution of conventional martensitic stainless steels with the aim of extending their applicability to more demanding service conditions, particularly in the oil and gas industry [ 36 ,  37 ]. By combining reduced carbon content with alloying additions such as nickel and molybdenum, these steels exhibit improved toughness, weldability and corrosion resistance when compared to traditional 13Cr martensitic grades, while maintaining lower production and processing costs than duplex and superduplex stainless steels and other corrosion resistant alloys (CRAs) [ 36 ,  38 ]. This balance of mechanical performance, corrosion resistance and cost-effectiveness has led to the widespread adoption of SMSS, commercially known as S13Cr steels, in the manufacturing of Oil Country Tubular Goods (OCTG), including tubing, casing and packer components used in oil and gas wells [ 37 ]. In OCTG applications, structural integrity is strongly influenced by the performance of threaded connections, which are responsible for joining tubular components and ensuring sealing and load transfer under complex service conditions. These threaded connections are produced by machining processes, making the surface integrity generated during manufacturing a critical factor for the functional reliability of the components [ 39 ]. In this context, machining-induced features such as residual stresses and surface roughness may significantly affect fatigue resistance, susceptibility to stress corrosion cracking and service life, particularly in environments containing CO₂, H₂S and chlorides [ 40 ,  41 ].

Despite the technological relevance of SMSS, studies addressing their machining behavior have predominantly focused on conventional turning operations, with emphasis on machinability, tool life and wear mechanisms [ 42 ,  43 ]. Duarte et al. [ 43 ]. investigated the machinability of a Ti-alloyed supermartensitic stainless steel (UNS S41426), evaluating the influence of cutting parameters and lubrication-cooling strategies during turning. Their results indicated that feed rate was the most influential parameter on surface roughness, while the dominant tool wear mechanisms were abrasion, attrition and diffusion. Corrêa et al. [ 42 ]. studied the turning of UNS S41426 supermartensitic stainless steel in comparison with UNS S41000 martensitic stainless steel, assessing tool life and wear mechanisms under different cutting conditions. The authors reported shorter tool life for the supermartensitic grade when higher cutting speeds, feeds and depths of cut were employed, with adhesion and abrasion identified as the predominant wear mechanisms. While these studies provide important insights into the machinability of supermartensitic stainless steels during turning, they remain limited to this single machining operation and do not address the residual stress state induced in the machined surface. Moreover, the influence of subsequent finishing processes, such as grinding and belt-finishing, has received little to no attention in the context of SMSS. In particular, the combined effects of turning and abrasive finishing operations on residual stresses and surface roughness have not yet been systematically investigated, representing a relevant gap in the current literature. Addressing this gap is essential for improving the understanding of surface integrity in machined SMSS components and for supporting the optimization of manufacturing processes applied to critical oil and gas applications.

The present work aims to investigate the residual stresses and surface roughness generated in the machining of supermartensitic stainless steel by turning, grinding and belt-finishing, under different cutting conditions. Surface and subsurface residual stresses were measured by X-ray diffraction, using the sin²ψ method and layer removal by electropolishing technique. The study was complemented by analyses of surface finish, characterized by the surface roughness (Ra) parameter.

The main contributions of the present study can be summarized as follows. First, it provides an experimental investigation of residual stresses and surface roughness induced by turning, grinding and belt-finishing of supermartensitic stainless steel, assessing the influence of cutting parameters and insert geometry on the behavior of both surface and subsurface residual stresses. Second, it evaluates the effectiveness of grinding and belt-finishing as post-turning finishing operations, allowing a direct comparison of their influence on the residual stresses and surface finish. These aspects are particularly relevant for supermartensitic stainless steel tubular components commonly joined by threaded connections manufactured by machining, where surface integrity plays a critical role in structural performance.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: This section details the material investigated, the machining experiments conducted, and the methods used for residual stress and surface roughness analyses. Owing to limitations in available resources and experimental infrastructure, complementary analyses such as cutting force measurements, temperature monitoring, detailed microstructural characterization. Consequently, the investigation was focused on experimental characterization through residual stress measurements by X-ray diffraction, surface roughness evaluation, and statistical analysis, which are directly related to the objectives of this work.

sections.heading: Workpiece material
paragraphs: In this work, a supermartensitic stainless steel of grade VM110CRSS (as given by Vallourec Soluções Tubulares do Brasil) was studied. The material was supplied in the form of cylindrical bars with a diameter of 12 mm and a machining length of 100 mm. The material was delivered in the quenched and tempered condition, however, detailed information regarding the specific heat treatment parameters was not disclosed by the manufacturer. The chemical composition and mechanical properties of the material are shown in Tables  1  and  2 , respectively.

sections.heading: Machining experiments
paragraphs: The cylindrical bars previously described correspond to an intermediate stage in the manufacturing of tensile test specimens, which are produced by machining. Therefore, the machining conditions adopted in this study were selected to be representative of those commonly employed during specimen fabrication, rather than arbitrary cutting conditions. This approach allows the residual stress state and surface finish generated during machining to be analyzed under conditions that are relevant to mechanical and electrochemical testing. The experimental procedure was organized in a sequential manner, combining turning, grinding and belt-finishing, as illustrated by the flowchart presented in Fig.  1 .
Fig. 1 Flowchart of the experiments and analyses

As described previously, Fig.  1  schematically illustrates the experimental sequence adopted in this study. Initially, twelve samples were turned, and the influence of cutting speed, feed rate and insert geometry on residual stresses and surface roughness was investigated. Subsequently, selected turned samples were submitted to finishing operations in order to evaluate their capability to modify the residual stress state induced by turning. Among the twelve turned samples, four were selected for grinding experiments and other four for belt-finishing experiments. For the grinding experiments, the influence of depth of cut on residual stresses and surface roughness was analyzed, whereas in the belt-finishing operation the effect of abrasive grain size was investigated. All machining experiments were performed under flood cooling conditions using a semi-synthetic cutting fluid.

The turning experiments were carried out on a CNC VEKER LVK-175 lathe. Six samples of the material were turned using conventional insert and other six samples were turned using wiper insert. A new cutting edge was used in each experiment in order to avoid the effect of wear. The cutting speed and the feed rate were varied while the depth of cut was kept constant for all experiments. The cutting conditions of the turning experiments are shown in Table  3 .

Table 3 Turning parameters Parameter Value Cutting speed (m/min) 60, 80 and 100 Feed rate (mm/rev) 0.1 and 0.2 Insert geometry Conventional (TNMG160404-MF2025) and Wiper (TNMX160404-WF2015) Depth of cut (mm) 1.0 (constant)

The selection of the cutting parameters for the turning experiments was based on a compromise between practical constraints imposed by the machine tool and workpiece dimensions, the recommendations provided by the cutting tool manufacturer, and cutting conditions reported in the literature for turning martensitic and supermartensitic stainless steels. Regarding the practical constraints, the diameter of the samples (12 mm), combined with the maximum spindle speed of the CNC lathe (3000 rpm), limited the maximum attainable cutting speed to approximately 113 m/min. In order to avoid operating the machine at its maximum rotational capacity, a maximum cutting speed of 100 m/min was adopted as the upper level. A lower level of 60 m/min and an intermediate level of 80 m/min were selected to allow the assessment of cutting speed effects within a representative and operationally safe range. The feed rate and depth of cut were defined based on the recommendations provided by the insert manufacturer. For the conventional insert, the recommended feed rate ranges from 0.05 to 0.30 mm/rev and the recommended depth of cut from 0.10 to 1.50 mm, whereas for the wiper insert the recommended feed rate ranges from 0.08 to 0.30 mm/rev and the depth of cut from 0.20 to 2.50 mm. In addition, the selected cutting conditions are consistent with values reported in the literature for the turning of martensitic and supermartensitic stainless steels. Corrêa et al. [ 42 ]. investigated cutting speeds between 100 and 200 m/min, feed rates of 0.20 and 0.35 mm/rev, and depths of cut of 1.0 and 2.0 mm, while Duarte et al. [ 43 ]. employed cutting speeds ranging from 80 to 200 m/min, feed rates of 0.10 and 0.30 mm/rev, and a constant depth of cut of 1.0 mm. The cutting parameters adopted in the present study therefore fall within ranges used in previous investigations, while being adapted to the specific constraints of the samples and experimental setup.

The grinding and belt-finishing experiments were conducted by Vallourec Soluções Tubulares do Brasil (the material supplier), using equipment and process conditions representative of those employed during the manufacturing of tensile test specimens. This approach ensured that the investigated finishing operations were consistent with practical industrial conditions and with the surface integrity requirements imposed on specimens used for mechanical testing.

The grinding experiments were carried out on a CNC Toyoda 03/2014 60 M cylindrical grinding machine, using vitrified Al 2 O 3  grinding wheel, which was dressed using a single grain diamond dresser before each experiment to avoid the effect of wear. All grinding operations were conducted under flood cooling conditions. The cutting conditions of the grinding experiments are shown in Table  4 .

Table 4 Grinding parameters Parameter Value Depth of cut (mm) 0.01 and 0.02 Workpiece speed (rpm) 500 (constant) Grinding wheel speed (m/s) 60 (constant) Grinding wheel longitudinal feed (mm/rev) 0.008 (constant) Grinding wheel abrasive material Al 2 O 3 Abrasive grit size (mesh) 180 Binder type Vitrified Binder hardness grade K Grinding wheel outer diameter (mm) 510

The selection of the grinding parameters, particularly the depth of cut, took into consideration both practical and methodological limitations. The grinding conditions had to remain within the range employed by the manufacturer during the finishing of tensile test specimens, in order to achieve the surface quality required for mechanical testing while respecting the geometric limitations imposed by the small diameter of the cylindrical samples. Consequently, relatively low depths of cut were adopted, namely 0.01 mm and 0.02 mm, which are representative of fine grinding operations applied to small components. Although specific studies addressing the grinding of supermartensitic stainless steels are scarce, an extensive review of the literature on grinding of steels with different mechanical properties reveals that a wide range of grinding depths has been investigated, typically spanning from very fine cuts on the order of a few micrometers up to several hundredths of a millimeter, depending on the grinding parameter and workpiece material properties. Reported values include depths as low as 0.005 mm in precision grinding operations and values exceeding 0.5 mm in more aggressive grinding regimes [ 20 ,  22 ,  23 ,  25 ,  26 ]. Within this context, the depths of cut adopted in the present work fall within the lower bound of values reported in the literature.

The belt-finishing experiments were carried out on a Materials Testing Center GR04 automatic longitudinal polisher, using abrasive belts with different abrasive sizes. The cutting conditions of the experiments are shown in Table  5 .
Table 5 Belt-finishing parameters Parameter Value Abrasive grit size (mesh) 200 and 600 Belt transverse feed (mm/s) 40 (constant) Applied load (kg) 0.8 (constant)

Similar to the grinding experiments, the belt-finishing parameters were selected within the range of values employed in the manufacturing of the test specimens, in order to ensure the required surface quality while respecting the geometric limitations imposed by the cylindrical specimens. For the belt-finishing experiments, the abrasive grain size was selected as the primary variable to be investigated. This choice was motivated by two main factors. First, abrasive grain size is the parameter effectively varied in the industrial finishing process used for specimen preparation, whereas other parameters remain constant. Second, abrasive grain size is widely recognized in the literature as the dominant factor governing surface roughness, plastic deformation mechanisms and residual stress generation during belt-finishing operations. The abrasive grain sizes adopted in this study correspond to the belt grades available for the industrial process at the time of testing. Although the number of available abrasive belts was limited, the selected grain sizes are consistent with ranges commonly reported in the literature for belt-finishing of steels. Previous studies have investigated abrasive belt grain sizes spanning from very fine grades to coarser grades intended for more aggressive material removal [ 30 ,  31 – 32 ,  35 ]. While specific studies addressing belt-finishing of supermartensitic stainless steels are scarce, the abrasive grain sizes used in the present work fall within the range reported for different steel grades and finishing conditions.

sections.heading: Surface residual stress analysis
paragraphs: After the machining experiments, the residual stresses were measured by X-ray diffraction technique, using the sin²ψ method. The analyses were carried out using an XStress3000 stress analyzer and the stresses were calculated by XTronic V1-0 software, with a measurement uncertainty of ± 15 MPa. A collimator with a diameter of 2 mm was employed, defining the irradiated area during the measurements as approximately 3.14 mm². The parameters used in the residual stress measurements are presented in Table  6 .

Table 6 Residual stress measurement parameters Collimator diameter (mm) 2 Diffraction angle 2 θ  (º) 156.41 Diffraction plane (hkl) (211) Radiation Crκα Wavelength λCrKα (Å) 2.291 X-ray tube current (mA) 6.7 X-ray tube voltage (kV) 30 Inclination angles  ψ  (º) 0.0, 20.7, 30.0, 37.7, 45.0 Exposure time (s) 25

The residual stress measurements were carried out at a single point on each specimen corresponding to each turning, grinding and belt-finishing experiments. The measurement point was positioned at the center of the machined length of the cylindrical samples, and stresses were evaluated along the longitudinal direction, corresponding to the tool feed direction during machining. Due to limitations related to sample availability, experimental time and resources, each residual stress value represents a single observation rather than an average of repeated measurements, that is, it was not possible to produce replicates. The uncertainty associated with the residual stress measurements was estimated as ± 15 MPa, as provided by the equipment manufacturer and calibration procedure. Accordingly, the error bars presented in the residual stress results correspond to the measurement uncertainty of the stress analyzer.

sections.heading: Subsurface residual stress analysis
paragraphs: Subsurface residual stress profiles were obtained by combining X-ray diffraction measurements with successive material removal by electrolytic polishing. The layer removal process was conducted manually using an aqueous electrolyte composed of saturated NaCl solution, glycerin and ethanol. Electrolytic polishing was carried out under an applied voltage of 30 V and a current of approximately 0.5 A. After each polishing step, the thickness of the removed layer was measured using a Mitutoyo Absolute digital indicator (model ID C112B), allowing micrometric control of the depth increments and the construction of residual stress profiles as a function of depth.

The subsurface residual stress measurements were performed at selected depths below the machined surface in order to characterize the stress gradients induced by the different machining operations. For the turning condition, subsurface residual stresses were evaluated on two samples, one turned with a conventional insert and one with a wiper insert, with the objective of assessing the influence of insert geometry on the depth of the affected layer. In this case, measurements were conducted at depths of 10, 20, 30 and 45 μm below the surface. For the grinding and belt-finishing conditions, subsurface residual stresses were measured on one sample ground with a depth of cut of 0.01 mm, one ground with a depth of cut of 0.02 mm, one sample finished by belt-finishing using an abrasive belt with grit size 200, and one using grit size 600. For these finishing conditions, residual stresses were evaluated at depths of 10, 20, 30, 50, 75 and 100 μm below the surface. In addition, subsurface residual stress measurements were performed on two samples finished by belt-finishing using grit size 600, one previously turned with a conventional insert and another one previously turned with a wiper insert, in order to evaluate the influence of the turning-induced stress state on the subsurface response after belt-finishing. Once again, the residual stresses were evaluated at depths of 10, 20, 30, 50, 75 and 100 μm below the surface. The selected depth increments were chosen to adequately capture the near-surface stress gradients typically associated with machining and finishing processes, while remaining compatible with the spatial resolution of the X-ray diffraction technique and the layer removal procedure. This approach allows a meaningful comparison of subsurface stress evolution between different machining conditions, without aiming at a continuous stress-depth reconstruction.

The residual stress relaxation associated with material removal is usually assumed to be negligible, since the thickness of each removed layer is very small compared to the sample dimensions. In addition, the electrolytic polishing procedure adopted in this work was restricted to a localized surface area of approximately 5 mm × 10 mm, which was isolated using a mask in order to ensure that only the region of interest was exposed to the electrolyte. This localized approach allows the controlled removal of material exclusively within the irradiated area used for X-ray diffraction measurements, while preserving the remaining volume of the specimen. Under these conditions, any stress redistribution induced by the layer removal process is expected to remain within the measurement uncertainty of the stress analyzer [ 44 ].

sections.heading: Surface roughness analysis
paragraphs: Surface roughness was evaluated after the machining and finishing operations using the arithmetic mean roughness parameter Ra. The measurements were performed with a Taylor Hobson Surtronic 25 surface roughness tester. Although roughness assessment of ground and belt-finished surfaces would be more properly conducted using a cutoff wavelength of  λc  = 0.25 mm and an evaluation length of 1.25 mm, this configuration did not yield stable and repeatable measurements with the available equipment. For this reason, a cutoff wavelength of  λc  = 0.8 mm and an evaluation length of 4.0 mm were adopted for all samples, and a Gaussian filter was applied to separate roughness and waviness components. This configuration was consistently applied to samples machined by turning, grinding and belt-finishing, allowing a uniform comparison of surface roughness among the different processing conditions. For each sample, ten roughness measurements were performed along the machined surface. The surface roughness value reported for each condition corresponds to the arithmetic mean of these measurements, while the associated error bars represent the corresponding standard deviation.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: This section presents and discusses the experimental results obtained from turning, grinding and belt-finishing of supermartensitic stainless steel, with emphasis on the resulting residual stresses and surface roughness Ra.

sections.heading: Effect of turning parameters and insert geometry on residual stresses
paragraphs: This subsection analyzes the influence of cutting parameters and insert geometry on the residual stresses induced by turning, considering both surface and subsurface stress distributions. The residual stresses in the axial direction were measured after turning of S13Cr steel using different cutting conditions. The results are shown in Fig.  2 .
Fig. 2 Residual stresses induced by turning

The results show that tensile residual stresses of lower magnitudes were induced by turning with wiper inserts and higher cutting speeds, while the residual stress of higher magnitude (320 MPa) was generated in the sample turned with a conventional insert and cutting speed of 80 m/min. According to Khan et al. [ 45 ]. the wiper geometry provides a longer contact between the tool and the workpiece, when compared to conventional geometry, which can cause higher plastic deformations. Thus, the combined effect of the higher plastic deformations and the cooling provided by the cutting fluid could explain the lower tensile residual stresses produced with the use of a wiper insert.

All the turning experiments resulted in tensile residual stresses, however, lower tensile stresses were induced by turning with wiper insert and lower feed (0.1 mm/rev). The results may suggest that turning with wiper insert was more effective in promoting a less detrimental state of residual stresses in the machined surface, when compared to the results obtained when using conventional insert.
Figure  3  presents surface plots of the residual stresses generated by turning, showing the overall behavior of the residual stresses with respect to insert geometry and cutting parameters.
Fig. 3 Surface plots of residual stresses induced by turning with ( a ) conventional insert and ( b ) wiper insert

It can be seen in Fig.  3 a that when turning with conventional insert less tensile residual stresses were induced using higher cutting speed and higher feed. Figure  3 b shows that turning with wiper insert caused less tensile residual stresses to be generated with higher cutting speed, but with lower feed. Sarnobat and Raval [ 14 ] reported a similar tendency for generating tensile residual stresses of lower magnitudes when turning with cutting speeds ranging from 60 m/min to 120 m/min. According to the authors, with a cutting speed of 60 m/min, the contact time between the workpiece and the cutting tool is long enough for more heat to diffuse to the workpiece. With a cutting speed of 120 m/min, higher material removal rate and shorter contact time between tool and the workpiece are obtained, which results in more heat being evacuated by the chip and less heat being diffused to the workpiece. Salman et al. [ 15 ]. also reported that higher material removal rates due to an increase in cutting speed could cause more heat to be evacuated by the chips, reducing the thermal effects related to tensile residual stresses. Regardless of the influence of cutting parameters, the results presented in Figs.  2  and  3  suggest that turning with wiper insert was more effective in promoting a less detrimental state of residual stresses.

Subsurface residual stresses were analyzed in two samples in which surface residual stresses of the same magnitude (240 MPa) were measured. The selected samples were turned with conventional and wiper inserts and four measurements of subsurface residual stresses were taken in each sample, in depths of 10, 20, 30 and 45 μm. The results are presented in Fig.  4 .
Fig. 4 Depth profiles of residual stresses after turning with conventional and wiper inserts

The depth profiles reveal that from a thin layer of 10 μm only compressive residual stresses were generated and these stresses progressively increase in magnitude until the depth of 45 μm. The subsurface residual stresses were more compressive in samples turned with a wiper insert, reaching the maximum value of 470 MPa in the depth of 45 μm. The thicker deformed layer produced by turning with wiper insert may suggest that this type of insert is capable of generating higher plastic deformations when compared to the conventional insert. This observation could explain the less tensile residual stresses generated in the surface.

sections.heading: Influence of grinding and belt-finishing on residual stresses
paragraphs: This subsection presents a discussion of the effects of grinding and belt-finishing as post-turning finishing operations on the residual stresses, highlighting differences between surface and subsurface behavior. Grinding and belt-finishing experiments were conducted with previously turned samples of S13Cr steel and the residual stresses in the axial direction were measured. The results are shown in Fig.  5 .
Fig. 5 Residual stresses induced by grinding and belt-finishing after turning

In opposition to the results obtained in the turning experiments, both finishing processes induced compressive residual stresses only, which is more desirable when considering the quality of a machined component. In the grinding experiments, compressive stresses were measured for both depths of cut investigated (0.01 and 0.02 mm), with values ranging between − 260 and − 480 MPa. Although no clear trend with depth of cut can be established from the present dataset, the results indicate that relatively small variations in depth of cut are sufficient to significantly modify the resulting residual stress state in grinding of supermartensitic stainless steel. Previous studies have reported that the residual stress state generated by grinding results from a balance between different process-related mechanisms. Ding et al. [ 17 ]. reviewed that increasing grinding severity, through parameters such as depth of cut or feed, may enhance plastic deformation imposed by abrasive grains, favoring the generation of compressive residual stresses, while excessive grinding severity may promote conditions associated with stress relaxation or tensile stress formation. Similarly, Gong et al. [ 16 ]. discussed that the balance between mechanical deformation and other grinding-related effects strongly depends on the specific combination of cutting parameters, which explains why different residual stress magnitudes can be obtained even within narrow parameter ranges. In a comparative study of hard turning and grinding of bearing rings, Jouini et al. [ 20 ]. showed that grinding generally induced compressive surface residual stresses, which were associated with improved fatigue performance. The authors emphasized that grinding parameters influenced not only the stress magnitude but also the near-surface stress distribution, reinforcing the sensitivity of residual stresses to relatively small variations in grinding conditions. Similarly, Zhang et al. [ 22 ]. compared dry hard turning and grinding and observed that grinding led to more favorable surface integrity conditions, including compressive residual stresses at the surface. Their results emphasized that the grinding process produced a residual stress state dominated by compressive stresses in the near-surface region, which the authors related to the predominance of mechanical interactions between abrasive grains and the workpiece material. Furno and Sosa [ 24 ] investigated surface integrity in grinding of ductile iron and reported that both cutting conditions and material characteristics significantly affected the resulting residual stress profiles. They demonstrated that compressive stresses were generally obtained under moderate grinding conditions and that variations in grinding parameters altered not only the magnitude but also the depth distribution of residual stresses. The results obtained in this work are consistent with previous investigations showing that compressive residual stresses can be generated over a wide range of grinding conditions, while their magnitude remains highly sensitive to relatively small changes in process parameters.

Regarding belt-finishing, high compressive surface residual stresses were measured for both abrasive belts tested (− 480 MPa for grit 200 and − 540 MPa for grit 600). This behavior is in agreement with studies reporting that belt-finishing processes tend to induce high compressive stresses due to the predominance of repeated mechanical interactions between abrasive grits and the workpiece surface under contact pressure. Wang et al. showed that dry belt-finishing applied after hard turning generated compressive residual stresses concentrated in the near-surface region, which they attributed to localized plastic deformation induced by successive abrasive contacts. Cherguy et al. [ 30 ]. reported that belt-finishing of carburized steels produced compressive residual stresses within the first tens of micrometers below the surface, with limited sensitivity of stress magnitude to abrasive grain size under otherwise similar finishing conditions. Numerical and experimental analyses by Bouktib and Khellouki [ 35 ] further demonstrated that the generation of compressive residual stresses during belt-finishing is mainly governed by the accumulation of plastic strain induced by repeated abrasive scratching, while variations in abrasive grain size primarily affect the depth of the affected layer rather than systematically increasing or decreasing stress magnitude. In light of these observations, the slightly more compressive value measured for the 600 grit belt in the present study should not be interpreted as a clear evidence that abrasive grit size alone governs the magnitude of surface residual stresses, considering that only one specimen was analyzed for each abrasive belt. Additional repetitions would be required to confirm any statistically valid relationship between abrasive size and surface residual stress magnitude.

Subsurface residual stresses in the longitudinal direction were measured in the samples used in the grinding and belt-finishing experiments. Two of the ground samples, which presented the higher surface compressive residual stresses, were selected for the analysis of subsurface residual stresses. Two of the samples used in the belt-finishing experiments were selected for comparison with the results obtained with the ground samples, one finished with abrasive of size 200 and the other finished with abrasive of size 600. The results are presented in Fig.  6 .
Fig. 6 Depth profiles of residual stresses after ( a ) grinding and ( b ) belt-finishing

The depth profiles presented in Fig.  6  reveal a clear difference between the subsurface residual stresses induced by grinding and belt-finishing processes. All the subsurface residual stresses after grinding were tensile and of low magnitudes, while belt-finishing induced compressive residual stresses in a thin layer of 10 μm, which decreased in magnitude in deeper layers, becoming tensile in the deepest layers. This result is in agreement with the observations of Bouktib and Khellouki [ 29 ], who state that belt-finishing operation induce compressive residual stresses on a thin layer of material.

It can be seen that the affected layer after belt-finishing with abrasive of size 600 (fine abrasive) was thicker than that produced by belt-finishing with abrasive of size 200 (coarse abrasive), as the subsurface residual stresses remained in compression until the depth of 75 μm. This result may suggest that belt-finishing with fine abrasive belt induced more compressive residual stresses when compared with those induce by belt-finishing with coarse abrasive belt. On the other hand, the subsurface residual stresses in the ground samples were almost the same, regardless of depth of cut, which may suggest that the penetration of grinding wheel did not influence the residual stresses significantly. These results suggest that belt-finishing process was more effective in promoting a beneficial state of residual stresses both in the surface and subsurface of the samples, when compared to grinding process.

sections.heading: Effect of turning conditions on surface roughness
paragraphs: In order to analyze the surface finish produced by the different processes, surface roughness Ra was measured after all experiments. The results are shown in Fig.  7 .
Fig. 7 Surface roughness Ra after turning with different cutting conditions

The results shown in Fig.  7  reveal that a better surface finish (lower Ra values) ​​was obtained with the use of wiper insert, when compared to the surface finish obtained with conventional insert. In addition, when turning with wiper insert, the lowest value of surface roughness Ra (0.7 μm) was obtained using the lowest feed (0.1 mm/rev) and the highest cutting speed (100 m/min). Conversely, the highest value of R a  (1.86 μm) was obtained when turning with conventional insert, highest feed (0.2 mm/rev) and lowest cutting speed (60 m/min). Figure  8  presents surface plots of the surface roughness measured after turning with conventional and wiper inserts.
Fig. 8 Surface plots of surface roughness Ra after turning with: ( a ) conventional insert and ( b ) wiper insert

It can be observed that there was a tendency towards lower Ra values ​​when turning with higher cutting speeds, while higher R a  values were measured in all samples turned with higher feed (0.2 mm/rev) and the increase in surface roughness with increasing feed was more expressive in samples turned with conventional insert. These results are in agreement with those obtained by Khan et al. [ 45 ]. in a similar work. According to these authors, the multi-radius geometry of wiper inserts produces a smoothing effect that reduces the roughness peaks formed by the insert nose on the machined surface, which results in a better surface finish (lower Ra) than that obtained when turning with conventional inserts.

sections.heading: Surface roughness after grinding and belt-finishing operations
paragraphs: The results of surface roughness after grinding and belt-finishing experiments are shown in Fig.  9 .
Fig. 9 Surface roughness Ra after grinding and belt-finishing

It is possible to observe that a better surface finish was obtained in the samples ground with higher depth of cut (0.02 mm), when compared to those ground with lower depth of cut (0.01 mm). In this work the difference between the surface finish obtained with higher and lower depth of cut was not expressive, indicating that the depth of cut did not influence significantly. Furthermore, it is possible to observe that the previous turning experiments did not influence the surface finishing obtained in the grinding experiments. The surface finish obtained by belt-finishing was excellent, with a low surface roughness R a  of 0.4 μm. However, more experiments would be necessary to evaluate the influence of abrasive size on the surface finish produced by belt-finishing, since there was no difference in the results obtained with the different sizes used in this work.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In the present work the residual stresses and surface finish produced by turning, grinding and belt-finishing of supermartensitic stainless steel were experimentally investigated. Based on the experimental results, the following conclusions can be summarized:

Turning induced predominantly tensile residual stresses at the surface, whose magnitude was strongly influenced by insert geometry and cutting parameters. The use of wiper inserts, combined with lower feed rates and higher cutting speeds, consistently resulted in lower tensile residual stresses, indicating a less detrimental surface condition. Regardless of insert geometry, turning produced compressive residual stresses in the subsurface, with magnitudes increasing with depth. However, samples turned with wiper inserts exhibited a more pronounced compressive subsurface stress state, suggesting a thicker plastically deformed layer and a more favorable residual stress distribution when compared to conventional inserts. Grinding effectively modified the residual stress state induced by turning, leading to compressive residual stresses at the surface for all investigated conditions, independently of the prior turning parameters. The maximum surface compressive stress (− 480 MPa) was obtained for the lower grinding depth of cut applied to a sample previously turned with a wiper insert. While surface residual stresses showed sensitivity to grinding depth of cut, subsurface stresses were characterized by low magnitudes and exhibited a transition to tensile values within a shallow layer below the surface, remaining close to zero at greater depths. This behavior indicates that, under the investigated conditions, grinding was effective in improving surface residual stresses but resulted in a limited and less stable beneficial subsurface stress state. Belt-finishing provided the most favorable residual stress condition among the investigated finishing processes. High compressive residual stresses were generated at the surface for both abrasive belts, with the highest value (− 540 MPa) obtained for the finer abrasive (grit 600) applied to a sample previously turned with a wiper insert. In the subsurface, belt-finishing promoted compressive residual stresses over a thicker and more stable affected layer when compared to grinding. The combination of wiper turning followed by belt-finishing with grit 600 resulted in compressive stresses persisting to greater depths, indicating a more homogeneous and mechanically dominated residual stress profile. From a surface finish perspective, both grinding and belt-finishing significantly improved surface roughness when compared to turning, yielding similar Ra values under the investigated conditions. In turning, the best surface finish was obtained using wiper inserts, lower feed rates and higher cutting speeds, with feed rate exerting a more pronounced influence on Ra than cutting speed.
